items.new: Of the names on this list of whale authors, only those after Owen ever saw living whales, and only one of them was a real professional harpooner and whaleman. I mean Captain Scoresby. On the separate subject of the Greenland or right whale, he is the best authority there is. But Scoresby knew nothing and says nothing of the great sperm whale, compared with which the Greenland whale is hardly worth mentioning. And let it be said here that the Greenland whale is a usurper on the throne of the seas. He is not even by any means the largest of the whales. Yet because his claims go back so far, and because of the profound ignorance that, until some seventy years ago, surrounded the then fabulous or utterly unknown sperm whale — an ignorance that to this day still reigns everywhere except in a few scientific retreats and whaling ports — this usurpation has been complete in every way. A look at nearly all the allusions to leviathan in the great poets of past days will satisfy you that the Greenland whale, without a single rival, was to them the monarch of the seas. But the time has at last come for a new proclamation. This is Charing Cross (where London's royal proclamations were read); hear this, good people all — the Greenland whale is deposed — the great sperm whale now reigns!

items.new: BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER III (Fin-Back). — Under this heading I count a monster which, under the various names of Fin-Back, Tall-Spout, and Long-John, has been seen in almost every sea, and is commonly the whale whose distant jet is so often spotted by passengers crossing the Atlantic on the New York packet routes. In the length he reaches, and in his baleen, the Fin-Back resembles the right whale, but he is less portly in girth and lighter in color, approaching olive. His great lips have a cable-like look, formed by the intertwisting, slanting folds of large wrinkles. His grand distinguishing feature, the fin from which he gets his name, is often a conspicuous object. This fin is some three or four feet long, growing vertically from the rear part of the back, angular in shape, and with a very sharp-pointed end. Even when not the slightest other part of the creature is visible, this isolated fin will at times be seen plainly projecting from the surface. When the sea is moderately calm and lightly marked with spherical ripples, and this gnomon-like fin stands up and casts shadows on the wrinkled surface, it may well be supposed that the watery circle around it somewhat resembles a dial, with its style (the dial's upright pointer) and wavy hour-lines engraved on it. On that Ahaz-dial (the sundial on which, in the Bible, the shadow miraculously went backward) the shadow often goes back. The Fin-Back is not gregarious. He seems a whale-hater, as some men are man-haters. Very shy; always going solitary; rising unexpectedly to the surface in the remotest and most sullen waters; his straight and single lofty jet rising like a tall misanthropic spear on a barren plain; gifted with such wondrous power and speed in swimming as to defy all present pursuit by man — this leviathan seems the banished and unconquerable Cain of his race, bearing as his mark that style upon his back. Because he has baleen in his mouth, the Fin-Back is sometimes grouped with the right whale in a theoretical species called Whalebone whales, that is, whales with baleen. Of these so-called Whalebone whales there would seem to be several varieties, most of which, however, are little known. Broad-nosed whales and beaked whales; pike-headed whales; bunched whales; under-jawed whales and rostrated whales — these are the fishermen's names for a few sorts.

items.new: BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER III (Narwhale), that is, Nostril whale. — Another instance of a curiously named whale, so named, I suppose, because his peculiar horn was originally mistaken for a peaked nose. The creature is some sixteen feet in length, while its horn averages five feet, though some exceed ten, and even reach fifteen feet. Strictly speaking, this horn is only a lengthened tusk, growing out from the jaw in a line slightly depressed from the horizontal. But it is only found on the sinister side — the left — which has an ill effect, giving its owner something like the look of a clumsy left-handed man. What precise purpose this ivory horn or lance serves, it would be hard to say. It does not seem to be used like the blade of the swordfish and billfish, though some sailors tell me that the Narwhale uses it as a rake for turning over the bottom of the sea for food. Charley Coffin said it was used as an ice-piercer; for the Narwhale, rising to the surface of the Polar Sea and finding it sheeted with ice, thrusts his horn up and so breaks through. But you cannot prove either of these guesses correct. My own opinion is that however the Narwhale may really use this one-sided horn — however that may be — it would certainly be very convenient to him as a paper-folder in reading pamphlets. I have heard the Narwhale called the Tusked whale, the Horned whale, and the Unicorn whale. He is certainly a curious example of the Unicornism to be found in almost every kingdom of animate nature. From certain cloistered old authors I have gathered that this same sea-unicorn's horn was in ancient days regarded as the great antidote against poison, and as such, preparations of it brought immense prices. It was also distilled into volatile salts for fainting ladies, the same way that the horns of the male deer are made into hartshorn. Originally it was in itself considered an object of great curiosity. Black Letter (that is, old books printed in Gothic type) tells me that Sir Martin Frobisher, on his return from that voyage when Queen Bess gallantly waved her jeweled hand to him from a window of Greenwich Palace as his bold ship sailed down the Thames — "when Sir Martin returned from that voyage," says Black Letter, "on bended knees he presented to her highness a prodigious long horn of the Narwhale, which for a long period after hung in the castle at Windsor." An Irish author asserts that the Earl of Leicester, on bended knees, likewise presented to her highness another horn, belonging to a land beast of the unicorn nature.

items.new: It is not the least among the strange things bred by the intense artificiality of sea customs that, while on the open deck some officers will, when provoked, carry themselves boldly and defiantly enough toward their commander, yet, ten to one, let those very officers go down the next moment to their customary dinner in that same commander's cabin, and at once their inoffensive, not to say apologetic and humble, air toward him as he sits at the head of the table is marvelous, and sometimes most comical. Why this difference? A problem? Perhaps not. To have been Belshazzar, King of Babylon, and to have been Belshazzar not haughtily but courteously — in that there certainly must have been some touch of worldly grandeur. But the man who presides in a rightly regal and intelligent spirit over his own private dinner table of invited guests — that man's unchallenged power and dominion of personal influence for the time being, that man's royalty of state, surpasses Belshazzar's, for Belshazzar was not the greatest. Whoever has once had his friends to dinner has tasted what it is to be Caesar. It is a witchery of social czarship that there is no withstanding. Now, if on top of this you add the official supremacy of a ship's captain, then by inference you will arrive at the cause of that peculiarity of sea life just mentioned.

items.new: Now, since the business of standing mastheads, ashore or afloat, is a very ancient and interesting one, let us enlarge on it here to some extent. I take it that the earliest masthead-standers were the old Egyptians, because in all my research I find none before them. For though their forebears, the builders of Babel, must doubtless have meant their tower to be the loftiest masthead in all Asia, or Africa either, yet since (before the final truck, the wooden cap at the very top of a mast, was put to it) that great stone mast of theirs may be said to have gone by the board in the dread gale of God's wrath, we cannot give these Babel builders priority over the Egyptians. And that the Egyptians were a nation of masthead-standers is an assertion based on the general belief among archaeologists that the first pyramids were founded for astronomical purposes — a theory singularly supported by the peculiar stair-like formation of all four sides of those buildings, by which, with prodigiously long liftings of their legs, those old astronomers used to climb to the apex and sing out for new stars, just as the lookouts of a modern ship sing out for a sail, or a whale just coming into sight. In Saint Stylites, the famous Christian hermit of old times, who built himself a lofty stone pillar in the desert and spent the whole latter part of his life on its summit, hoisting his food up from the ground with a tackle — in him we have a remarkable instance of a dauntless masthead-stander, who was not to be driven from his place by fogs or frosts, rain, hail, or sleet, but, valiantly facing everything out to the last, literally died at his post. Of modern masthead-standers we have only a lifeless set: mere stone, iron, and bronze men, who, though well able to face out a stiff gale, are still entirely incompetent at the business of singing out on discovering any strange sight. There is Napoleon, who stands with arms folded on top of the column of Vendome, some one hundred and fifty feet in the air, careless now who rules the decks below, whether Louis Philippe, Louis Blanc, or Louis the Devil. Great Washington, too, stands high aloft on his towering main-mast in Baltimore, and like one of Hercules' pillars, his column marks that point of human grandeur beyond which few mortals will go. Admiral Nelson, also, stands his masthead on a capstan of gun-metal in Trafalgar Square; and even when he is most obscured by that London smoke, there is still a token that a hidden hero is there; for where there is smoke, there must be fire. But neither great Washington, nor Napoleon, nor Nelson will answer a single hail from below, however madly they are invoked to help with their counsel the distracted decks they gaze down on — however it may be surmised that their spirits penetrate the thick haze of the future and see what shoals and what rocks must be avoided.
